about.metaDescription: Who we are, how our yurt trips work and how booking works at NomadTrip.
about.title: About NomadTrip
about.intro: We organise yurt journeys across Kyrgyzstan, from two-day escapes to a full month in the Tian Shan.

who.1: NomadTrip is a small team that sends travellers into the Kyrgyz mountains and steppe, with every night spent in a traditional yurt camp.
who.2: We work directly with herder families and local guides, so the people you meet are the people who live and work in these valleys.

1.title: Small groups
1.body: Departures are kept small, so camps stay quiet and you are a guest at a family's table, not part of a crowd.

2.title: Nomad host families
2.body: Camps are run by local families who graze their animals on the summer pastures. They cook, host and share their way of life with you.

3.title: Local guides
3.body: Every trip has a guide who knows the route, the weather and the people, and who helps with language and customs.

1.title: Send a request
1.body: Choose a trip and a departure date, then tell us how many travellers you are. The request is not a payment.

2.title: We confirm within 24 hours
2.body: We check seats and details with our local partners and confirm your booking by email.

3.title: Receive payment details
3.body: Once confirmed, we send you the payment details and next steps.

about.bookingNote: If something is unclear, contact us before you book and we will help.

yurtLife.metaDescription: What a night in a Kyrgyz yurt is like, how to behave as a guest and what to pack.
yurtLife.title: Yurt life
yurtLife.intro: A yurt, or boz üy, is the traditional home of Kyrgyz herders. Here is what to expect.

1.title: The shanyrak
1.body: The wooden ring at the top of the roof is the shanyrak, a symbol of the Kyrgyz home. It lets in light and smoke, and at night you may see the stars through it.

2.title: Tushuk mattresses
2.body: You sleep on tushuks, thick felt-and-wool mattresses laid on the floor, with blankets provided. They are warm and more comfortable than they look.

3.title: The stove
3.body: Many yurts have a small stove for the evening. Camps usually light it at night when it gets cold.

4.title: Toilets and washing
4.body: Camps usually have shared toilets and, at some, simple shared showers. Facilities are basic and vary between camps, especially in the high mountains.

5.title: Cold nights
5.body: At altitude, nights are cold even in summer, and temperatures can drop close to freezing at the highest camps. Bring warm layers.

1.title: Shoes off
1.body: Take off your shoes before stepping onto the felt floor of a yurt.

2.title: Seating
2.body: Sit where your host invites you. The place opposite the door is for honoured guests. Avoid pointing your feet at others or at the hearth.

3.title: Bread
3.body: Bread is respected in Kyrgyz homes. Do not drop it or leave it face down, and eat what you take.

4.title: Kymyz
4.body: Fermented mare's milk may be offered as a gesture of welcome. You may politely decline or take just a sip.

pack.1: Warm layers and a warm hat for cold nights
pack.5: A sleeping-bag liner, if you like

faq.metaDescription: Answers about altitude, weather, fitness, kids, diets, horses, connectivity, money and visas.
faq.title: Frequently asked questions
faq.intro: Quick answers to the questions we hear most.

1.q: How high do the trips go?
1.a: Some trips reach high mountain lakes and passes at around 3,000 m or more, such as Song-Kul at about 3,000 m. Travel slowly on the first day and drink water. If you have heart, lung or other health concerns, talk to your doctor first.

2.q: What is the weather like and when should I go?
2.a: The best season for high-altitude camps is June to September. Days can be warm and nights cold, and weather in the mountains changes quickly, so bring layers.

3.q: How fit do I need to be?
3.a: Each trip lists a difficulty level. Easy trips involve gentle walks and rides. Challenging trips involve long days, rough roads or trekking at altitude.

4.a: Many easy trips suit families. Facilities in camps are basic, so choose a trip that fits your children's age and tell us about them when you book.

5.q: Can you cater for special diets?
5.a: Tell us about vegetarian, allergy or other dietary needs when you book. Traditional meals include a lot of meat, bread and dairy, and options in remote camps can be limited, so early notice helps.

6.a: Yes. Horses on our trips are used to beginners, and a local handler helps. Tell us your experience level and any concerns.

7.q: Will I have phone signal and internet?
7.a: Coverage is good near towns but often absent in high valleys and at remote camps. Expect to be offline for some of the trip.

8.q: How do money and cards work?
8.a: Cards are accepted in cities, but camps and villages mostly use cash in Kyrgyz som. Carry some cash and ask us if you are unsure.

9.a: Entry rules depend on your nationality and change over time. Please check the official Kyrgyz government or consular sources, or ask your embassy.

10.q: What about payment terms and cancellation?
10.a: Contact us before booking to ask about payment terms and what happens if your plans change. We will explain how they apply to your trip.

faq.contactNote: Still have a question? Contact us and we will help.
